newsitem.title: UK: Derivative knowhow can be dangerous thing - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Derivative knowhow can be dangerous thing - analysts.

text.p: High-profile losses may have sent senior managers scurrying to learn the minutiae of derivatives, but that approach could hinder rather than help companies manage their risk, industry analysts and officials said.

Robert Baldoni, a partner in Ernst & Young LLP's risk management and regulatory practice told Reuters the pendulum had swung too far towards expecting company executives to understand complicated products.
"There tends to be a double standard when it comes to derivatives," said Baldoni, a New York-based analyst recently in London for risk strategy meetings.
"In an industrial company, many people on the board have no idea how products are made...but that's acceptable," he said.
"But when it gets to derivatives a non-financial executive is expected to construct the yield curve on a swap. That's not an acceptable approach."

Companies have been under pressure to keep a firm hand on derivatives activities in the wake of debacles such as the collapse of Barings in 1995. The blue-blooded British merchant bank caved in under the weight of nearly $1.4 billion in losses caused by unauthorised derivatives deals by trader Nick Leeson.
The list of derivatives disasters runs long and dates well back into the 1980s.
From Orange County, California to Volkswagen in Germany to Kashima Oil Co in Japan, derivatives have been the medium for a series of trading mishaps that have led to multi-million-dollar losses.

But expecting specialist knowledge in reaction to those losses could slow the whole process of adding sophisticated risk management, by setting a standard that it is impossible for many executives to meet, analysts said.
"Getting senior management to that very technical level is not where their value is. Their value is in financial governance, or oversight," Baldoni said.
"The system will grind to a halt, to try and get those people up to speed on the technicals."

Gay Evans, chairman of the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA), said that the most important issue for board members was that they should be aware of overall risk -- including the nature of their derivatives activities and the legal implications -- without getting bogged down in the intricacies.
"Boards need to have a bigger perspective than that," she said. "If they have a good grasp of risk, they will then establish and have appropriate policies and procedures to protect themselves."
She said that appreciation of risk would lead to more effective management than attempts by boards to follow the ins and outs of individual transactions.
Baldoni said companies should focus on developing formal oversight procedures and responsibilities, which avoid giving too free a rein to a single individual.
Establishing a control infrastructure and ensuring it is adhered to should be a priority for companies, so that alarm bells start ringing long before money is lost, he said.
